STATEMENTS OF INTEREST 1
 The Pacific Justice Institute (PJI) is a non- profit
legal organization established under § 501(c)(3) of the
Internal Revenue Code. Since 1997, PJI has advised
and represented in court scores of religious
institutions and individuals of varying faiths in
religious liberty matters. Throughout the last decade
alone, PJI addressed matters impacting Christians,
Jews, Muslims, Taoists, Christian Scientists,
Jehovah’s Witness, and Buddhists, to name a few.
Each one of these religious groups desire the freedom
to live and worship according  to the dictates of their
conscience.
 PJI has an institutional interest in safeguarding
the First Amendment rights of all religious groups,
and thus desires that  the Court address the tensions
between the First Amendment protections and the
zoning process.   I ndeed, PJI understands that
persecution upon one faith can easily lead to
persecution of others.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
 Liberty of Conscience is part of the human
condition. In 1689, John Locke believed that liberty of
conscience was every man’s natural right.  See
Jonathan Barth, Liberty of Conscience is Every Man’s
Natural Right; Historical Background on the First
Amendment, 35 J. Pol’y Hist. 436,438 (2023).

1No counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in
part. No person or entity other than amici and their counsel
made a monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation
or submission of this brief.

2


According to the Religious Freedom Institute,
“Religious freedom is therefore the right of all persons
to believe, speak, and act –  individually and in
community with others, in private and in public –  in
accord with their understanding of ultimate truth.”
See Religious Freedom Institute, “What in the World
is Religious Freedom?”
https://religiousfreedominstitute.org/?s=%22What+in
+the+world+is+religious+freedom%22 (Last visited
September 6, 2026).
 When one speaks of religious liberty, each person
desires the ability to practice the beliefs that are part
of their inner being. It entails the freedom to believe
or not believe in a particular faith or creed. If state
actors do not adequately protect the free exercise
rights of all faith communities, the country will
witness more religious persecution.
 No human really wants to be told how to practice
their faith. No one wants to feel that their house
sanctuary is threatened because their faith practices
are not accepted in the local community. Yet, this is
what one sees not just in America but around the
world in the Jewish, Muslim, and Christian
communities.  Some faith communities must act with
caution when having their bibles viewed around local
government authorities.
 The United States of America is considered a land
of freedom because this country believes in liberty of
conscience. Daniel Grand was practicing his sincerely
held religious belief in having prayer sessions in his
home with other Jewish brethren on Friday evenings.
Mr. Grand should not have to live the rest of his days
wondering whether he can comfortably pray in his

3


home or need to look over his shoulders for potential
agitators seeking to restrict his free exercise rights.
ARGUMENT
I. AS MORE RELIGIOUS LIBERTY
PROTECTIONS ARE WITHDRAWN, FAITH
COMMUNITIES WILL SUFFER.
a. Recent reports on the state of religious liberty
in America indicate progression in some states
and regression in others.
Religious liberty is a lifestyle. Where one chooses
to work or reside; who one chooses to marry or simply
befriend; what one chooses to wear, eat or read; how a
person chooses to live their life – all are really folded
into a person’s faith walk or spirituality.  For many,
that also includes worship.  One faith community may
choose to worship outside in nature, exploring the
mountainside. Another faith community may choose
to worship in a religious building which may be a
church, temple or mosque.  Indeed, for many others,
when a nature walk is not feasible or a religious
building is unattainable, sometimes, the last option
available is a family home.  Praying at home  was
Daniel Grand’s last option, and he wanted to utilize
his home for his fellow Jewish brethren in the
community.
In a country like the United States of America,
founded on principles of freedom that make up the
core of who we are as a country, one would assume
that we have all of the religious protections available.
Yet, various reports on the status of religious liberty
in America demonstrate that our country has not fully

4


realized the aspirations enumerated in the First
Amendment’s religion clauses.   Take, for example, a
recent 2026 Religious Liberty in the States report,
produced by First Liberty’s Center for Religion,
Culture, & Democracy. Within this report, various
laws from each state have been reviewed to assess
where the state ranked in terms of religious liberty
protections.  What one  notices is that over the years,
some states have improved their religious liberty
protections for their citizens. For example, the state of
Ohio was ranked seventh for the various laws the
state has in place for protecting the religious liberty
rights of its citizens.  But other states like New York
have regressed, currently ranked fiftieth due to the
level of restrictions and lack of accommodations for
people of faith. See First Liberty Institute’s Center for
Religion, Culture, & Democracy, Religious Liberty in
the States –  2026;
https://religiouslibertyinthestates.com/downloads/
(Last visited on September 2, 2026)
In 2025, a Pew Research report showed that many
Americans believe that there is still a significant level
of discrimination faced by the Jewish and Muslim
communities here on American soil. Of those
surveyed, a 57% majority of adults state that people
who are relig ious are “subject to  a lot or some
discrimination.”  When asked about specific religious
groups, most believed that Jews and Muslims faced
more discrimination compared to evangelicals. See
Pew Research, “How Much Discrimination Do
Americans Say  Groups Face  in the U.S. ?” Report -
May 20, 2025,
https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/05/20/how

5


-much-discrimination-do-americans-say-groups-facein-the-u-s/.
The travesty for Daniel Grand is that because of
the level of discrimination present in his town, it is
likely that he and other Jewish brethren have to look
over their shoulders before engaging in the free
exercise of their sincerely held religious beliefs. Some
people may say that th is is merely politics.  Others
may say that this is outright antisemitic  attitudes.
Either way, what is happening to Mr. Grand is wrong.
The issues are ripe and this C ourt should have this
case remanded for further proceedings.
b. Multiple faith groups have been persecuted
overseas, some after being  labeled “extremist”
in their religious views; and this could happen
in America when the government or even one
faith community is not accepting of another
faith community.
Although comparison to  other countries  has its
analytical drawbacks,  it is self -evident that many
faith groups are not as privileged to have the religious
freedom protections that the United States currently
affords. Some countries have drawn up designated
lists for faiths that are deemed to be “ extremist” in
their religious views. For example, in 2017, Jehovah’s
Witnesses were declared to be an extremist group in
Russia. Because the government permitted such
designations, this particular faith community had
their houses of worship permanently closed. More
recently, on July 31, 2026, the Kuzminskiy District
Court of Moscow ordered those multiple properties

6


belonging to the Jehovah’s Witnesses be confiscated
and transferred over to the government of the Russian
Federation.  See  JW.org, “Moscow Court Orders
Seizure of 123 Properties Owned by European
Entities of Jehovah’s Witnesses”
https://www.jw.org/en/news/region/russia/Russian-
Authorities-Seize-123-Properties-Owned-by-
Jehovahs-Witnesses/ (last visited September 4, 2026)
and Andrew Osborn,“Russian Seizes Jehovah
Witnesses’ Properties , News Nation, July 31, 2026
https://www.newsnationnow.com/religion/russiaseizes-jehovahs-witnesses-properties/.
According to another Pew Research report from
June 2026, in 2023 Spain and Norway also witnessed
increased attacks against Jehovah’s Witnesses,
Muslims, and Jews varying from in- person verbal
harassment to hate speech on social media platforms.
See Samirah Majumdar and Vivian Jacobs, “More
Countries Had Elevated Levels of Social Hostilities
Involving Religion in 2023” , Pew Research Center,
June 2026,  doi: 10.58094/CV0D -0488
https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2026/06/15/mor
e-countries-had-elevated-levels-of-social-hostilitiesinvolving-religion-in-2023/.
Mr. Grand himself experienced similar hostilities
towards his faith, simply by wanting to have a prayer
session in his home on Friday evenings.
Further, for Christians in countries like China,
Cuba, Eritrea, and Brunei the main persecutor is the
government.  See The Voice of the Martyrs, Global

2026).   In many instances, even the bibles purchased
for distribution are being tracked and monitored.
The loss of religious liberty for minority faiths does
not typically begin with persecution; it starts with
subtle discrimination.  In the deliberations over the
Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act,
the senator who introduced the bill was a Republican
and a Mormon.  He partnered with a ranking senate
Democrat –who was a Roman Catholic –  to issue a
statement regarding the need for federal protections.
They wrote, “Churches and synagogues cannot
function without a physical space adequate to their
needs and consistent with their theological
requirements.”  146 Cong. Rec. S7774- 01 (daily ed.
July 27, 2000) (Joint Statement of Senator Hatch and
Kennedy on the Religious Land Use and
Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000).  Although the
Joint Statement was published a quarter century ago,
they could have been speaking about someone like Mr.
Grand.  Moreover, in enacting RLUIPA, its chief
proponents stated that they were seeking to counter
subtle discrimination that “lurks behind such vague
and universally applicable reasons as traffic,
aesthetics, or ‘not consistent with the city’s land use
plan.’” Id.  Here, officials from the City of University
Heights stand in the shoes of the generation before
them in using seemingly neutral rules as a tactic to
keep out an unwanted religious group.  RLUIPA was
enacted to prevent such discrimination which if left

9


unchecked can metastasize into state -sponsored
persecution.
In Mr. Grand’s case, the City of University Heights
had local residents that engaged in surveillance of Mr.
Grand and his property.  This was followed by a series
of complaint letters to the mayor about Mr. Grand’s
supposed activities on his own property. See Grand v.
City of University Heights,  No. 1:22-cv-1594 *11, 14
2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 176340 * (N.D. OH. Sept. 30,
2024). Shortly thereafter, Mr. Grand was admonished
by the municipality to end his weekly prayer sessions.
Should individuals in Daniel Grand’s position and
other faith groups now be concerned about their free
exercise rights because the local government and  a
majority of residents object to having a minority faith
group in their community?  Your amicus proffers that
state actors should be more vigilant in protecting free
exercise rights of religious adherents in the fac e of
community hostility – not less.  This remains true of
minority faiths so long as their exercise does not
interfere with peace, safety and morals.  Thus ,
enjoyment of religious liberty cannot be put up for a
community vote or consensus at a city council or
planning commission meeting.
Caving into the hostile shouts of local citizens or
the religious bigotry of state actors will send
communities down the same dark path commonly
witnessed in countries with authoritarian regimes.

10


II. BUILDING A BRIDGE BETWEEN CHURCH
AND STATE COULD NEGATIVELY IMPACT
DANIEL GRAND’S FREE EXERCISE RIGHTS.
Within the past few years, there has been much
commentary on church and state relations.  One
common theme that has been proclaimed throughout
the United States, and even other parts of the world,
is that the world is morally in flux because God is not
in government.  Many Americans believe that
government policies impact moral values.  See
Armstrong Williams, “When Civilizations lose God,
they eventually lose themselves” , Fox Baltimore 45
News, May 26, 2026,
https://foxbaltimore.com/news/armstrong-armystrong/when-civilizations-lose-god-they-eventuallylose-themselves; and
https://news.gallup.com/poll/710648/americansrating-moral-values-hits-new-low.aspx; Megan
Brenan, “Americans’ Rating of Moral Values Hits a
New Low,”  Gallup, Inc., May 28, 2026,
https://news.gallup.com/poll/710648/americansrating-moral-values-hits-new-low.aspx; and Chip
Rotolo and Gregory A. Smith, “How Americans Feel
about Religion’s Influence in Government and Public
Life,”  Pew Research Center, May 2026,
https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2026/05/14/how
-americans-feel-about-religions-influence-ingovernment-and-public-life/.
Other thoughts include the idea that there are not
enough individuals attending regular weekly church

11


services; and there are not enough God -fearing men
and women in government.  Therefore, let us have
church and state come together to bring the United
States to higher ground morally.   Similar sentiments
were expressed in the 17 th century, with the belief
that if God was in government, the country would fare
better. See Jack L. Arnold, “Church History: The
Church in America 17th Century – The Modern
Church Part 8,” Biblical Perspectives Magazine
(Third Millennium Ministries)
https://thirdmill.org/magazine/article.asp/link/jac_ar
nold%5ECH.Arnold.CH.35.html/at/The%20Church%
20in%20America:%2017th%20Century (Last visited
Sept. 6, 2026).
In June 2026, The Presidential Religious Liberty
Commission presented a draft report on the state of
religious liberty in the United States.  After a series
of hearings involving testimony from various
individuals, including politicians and faith- based
leaders, several r ecommendations were made on the
importance of safe-guarding religious freedom.  Those
recommendations covered categories including, but
not limited to , Faith-based Institutions, Education,
Parental Rights in Education, Healthcare, and
Antisemitism. See U.S. Dep’t of Justice, Religious
Liberty Commission, Draft Report - the Presidential
Religious Liberty Commission , pg. 13 -23 (2026) ,
chromeextension://efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https:

12


//www.justice.gov/religious-libertycommission/media/1449896/dl?inline.
Although the draft report acknowledged that
“Religious Liberty is for Everyone,” ( Id. at 29), the
report goes further by indicating a desire to build a
bridge between God and Government, which refers to
church and state. Id. at 36-44. Building even a bridge
between church and state could negatively impact
Daniel Grand’s free exercise rights, because in the
process of building, municipalities will inevitably
appease some faith groups at the expense of others.
See Jesus Christ is the Answer Ministries, Inc. v.
Baltimore County , 915 F.3d 256, 262- 264 (4th Cir.
2019).  Minority faiths will suffer.
One of the reasons why this court’s decision in Mr.
Grand’s case is important is because the City of
University Heights  believed that they could dictate
how Mr. Grand could use his own home for prayer
sessions. Based upon some of the court filings in the
case, the municipality appeared to have heavily relied
upon local resident informants on what they believed
to be Mr. Grand’s home activities prior to issuing their
cease-and-desist letter to Mr. Grand.  See Grand v.
City of University Heights,  No. 1:22-cv-1594 *11, 14
2024 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 176340 * (N.D. OH. Sept. 30,
2024).  In addition, there were allegations that the
neighborhood would be too loud on Fridays because of
all of the individuals driving to Mr. Grand’s home.
Yet, this is  false because during the Sabbath hours,

13


the Jewish brethren walk to their destination.  Many
of those same informants expressed in writing that
they did not want Jews in their community.
Building a bridge between church and state is only
a formality to forming a complete union. If a
municipality can start determining which faiths can
and cannot worship in their town, church and state
has formed a union.  Minority faiths will feel the
impact the most, because they will be considered
outside of what is deemed  normal, comfortable, and
acceptable in their community at large.  Furthermore,
the country could witness more examples of blatant
discrimination similar to what has been endured by
Mr. Grand.  See Pew Research, “How Much
Discrimination Do Americans Say Groups Face in the
U.S.?” Report -  May 20, 2025,
https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2025/05/20/how
-much-discrimination-do-americans-say-groups-facein-the-u-s/.
III. HISTORICAL NARRATIVES DEMONSTRATE
THAT GOVERNMENT INTERFERENCE WITH
FAITH WILL LEAD TO PERSECUTION.
What constitutes “persecution” may vary
depending on who m one asks.  Recently, the Ninth
Circuit Court was asked to address an immigration
matter for a woman where the meaning  of religious
persecution was at issue .   In Silva v. Bondi, 139 F.
4th 1137, 1143 (9th Cir. 2025), the court noted that
persecution can be emotional, psychological, and
physical. See Mashiri v. Ashcroft, 383 F.3d 1112, 1120
(9th Cir. 2004).  The court recognized that the

14


“Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the
Human Rights Covenant proclaim the right to
freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, which
right includes the freedom of a person to manifest [her
religion] in public or private, in teaching, practice,
worship and observance.” See Zhang v. Ashcroft,, 388
F.3d 713, 720 (9th Cir. 2004), as cited in Silva, 139 F.
4th at 1143.
Persecution at the hands of the government dates
back to biblical times. In the Holy Bible, the book of
Daniel (believed by many scholars to have been
written in the 6th century, B.C.)2 details the story of
three Hebrew men: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
(better known by their Babylonian names as
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego) 3 who refused to
bow down to a golden image set up by King
Nebuchadnezzar. Their refusal in bowing to the image
lead to persecution in a fiery furnace. See Daniel 3:12,
20-21 (King James).
Daniel, himself, was subject to persecution  for
continuing his prayers to the God of Heaven, despite
a royal statute established by governors, princes,
counsellors and captains who came together to
primarily persecute Daniel  for his faith . See Daniel
6:4-16 (King James) . Daniel regularly opened his

windows and prayed to the God of Heaven in private;

The chief priests and elders took counsel to put
Jesus Christ to death. Jesus stood trial before Pontius
Pilate and had a hearing before Herod Antipas all
because Jesus chose to proclaim the good news of
salvation. See Matthew 26:57- 75; Matthew 27:1- 30;
and Luke 23:1- 25 (King James) .   These biblical
examples demonstrate what happens when religion
(church) and the government (state) come together to
unduly interfere with the free exercise of faith.
One would truly believe that over time, and after
reviewing and (for some) living through history, the
sympathy and empathy of mankind would have
evolved; that the spirit of love and benevolence would
have permeated the heart and soul.  Not so. The
historical record and current events instead provide a
dark record of intolerance.
During the colonial period there was religious
freedom – for those who belonged to the majority
church.  Seventeenth century Puritan communities
whipped Baptist preachers and hung Quakers.
Michael W. McConnell, Establishment and
Disestablishment at the Founding, Part I:
Establishment of Religion , 44 Wm. & Mary L. Rev.
2105, 2162 (2003).  Virginia barred Catholic priests
and two dissenting ministers (i.e., non-Anglican) were
sentenced to thirty -one lashes for baptizing children
without a license.  Id. at 2164.  Virginia authorities

16


also jailed Baptist preachers for preaching without a
license.  Both South Carolina and Georgia prohibited
Catholic Churches.  Id. at 2166.  Georgia, New Jersey,
New Hampshire, and South Carolina limited the
holding of political office to Protestants.  Id. at 2179.
North Carolina excluded those who “denied…the
truth of the Protestant religion.”  The more liberal
Delaware simply required a belief in the Trinity.  Id.
at 2178.  These examples are not outliers and
certainly not an exhaustive list of religious
intolerance.
In contrast to what was the historical norm , the
First Amendment reflects the American experiment of
religious tolerance as an attempted exception.  When
followed through, this experiment works remarkably
well.  The Founders were very cognizant of the
carnage brought by the 16 th and 17 th century
European Wars of Religion which sought coercive
spiritual unity.  Hence, not only the religion clauses of
the Fir st Amendment, but also Article VI (“no
Religious Test shall ever be required as a qualification
to any office or public trust under the United States”)
pivot from the impulse to compel religious uniformity
by violence or force of law.  See Leslie C. Griffin,
Fighting the new wars of religion: the need for a
tolerant First Amendment,  62 Me. L. Rev. 23, 28- 32
(2010).
Fast forward to modern America where
individuals of differing faiths  can freely  maintain

17


their sincerely held religious beliefs in the way they
learn, work, live, and worship.  But the record here
shows something quite different.  Instead of allowing
Mr. Grand to live his life and be a blessing to his fellow
Jewish brethren, providing a refuge for Friday
evening prayer, municipal authorities –  with the aid
of disgruntled local residents – chose to suppress Mr.
Grand’s free exercise rights.
The Religious Land Use and Institutionalized
Persons Act was crafted to make a course adjustment
back to the aspirations enumerated in the religion
clauses such that the bigotry of a government official
or the howls of the crowd –  exercising the mob rule
that the drafters of the Constitution feared – would be
constrained.
